summary: Describes an architecture for measuring and reporting network traffic flows and how it fits into a larger traffic flow architecture. It was experimental, and it was replaced by RFC 2722.

eli5.summary: Counting cars that pass by a road by type, to see where the traffic comes from and goes. This describes a system for doing that for network traffic.

questions: how to measure network traffic flows
subtitle: How to measure and report network traffic flows in Internet networks

tldr.problem: Network operators need a standard way to measure how much traffic flows through their networks, where it comes from, and where it goes, for capacity planning and billing.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a general architecture where specialized meters at strategic points in the network classify traffic into flows, readers collect the flow data, managers configure the system, and analysis applications produce reports.
tldr.outcome: It was experimental and was succeeded by RFC 2722, which refined the traffic measurement architecture. This approach became foundational for network traffic analysis.

today: RFC 2722 replaced this experimental architecture with a refined version. RFC 2063 laid important groundwork for network traffic measurement that was adopted in real traffic measurement systems and SNMP-based monitoring tools.

sections.title: Overview of Traffic Flow Measurement
sections.content:
Network traffic flow measurement provides a way to understand network behavior for planning, performance analysis, and accounting. RFC 2063 defines an architecture — not a specific protocol — for measuring and reporting network traffic flows consistently across different equipment, protocols, and network layers.

The key insight is that traffic can be classified into flows: logical collections of packets sharing common attributes (such as the same source and destination addresses). By counting packets and bytes in each flow over time, network operators gain insight into traffic patterns, can identify capacity bottlenecks, verify service quality, and attribute usage to users for billing purposes.
sections.eli5: This RFC is about a system to count and track Internet traffic. Instead of counting all packets together, it groups them into flows (like different conversations) and counts each flow separately.

sections.title: The Four-Component Architecture
sections.content:
The traffic flow measurement system consists of four main components that interact with each other:

Meters are placed at measurement points in the network (typically in routers or on network links). Each meter observes passing packets, classifies them into flows according to configurable rules, and maintains a flow table with aggregate counts (packets and bytes) for each flow.

Meter Readers reliably collect usage data (flow records) from meters at regular intervals, extracting the accumulated counts and sending them to storage or analysis systems.

Managers are applications that configure meters with rules specifying which flows to measure, set parameters like inactivity timeouts, and control meter readers to determine what data to collect and how often.

Analysis Applications process the collected flow data to produce reports such as traffic matrices (flows between pairs of networks), usage summaries by host or user, and traffic distribution graphs for understanding network behavior.
sections.eli5: The system has four jobs: a meter counts the traffic, a reader collects the counts, a manager tells them what to do, and an application makes sense of the numbers.

sections.title: Defining Flows and Measuring Granularity
sections.content:
A traffic flow is an artificial grouping of packets with common attribute values, such as packets between the same pair of IP addresses. Flow attributes include addresses at various network layers (physical, link, network, transport), interface numbers, timestamps of first and last packet seen, and counters of packets and bytes in both directions (forward and reverse).

The granularity of flow measurement is the trade-off between overhead and detail. A coarse granularity (fewer, larger flows) reduces meter memory and processing. A fine granularity (many small flows) provides more detailed reports. Granularity is controlled by adjusting which attributes define a flow, how they are masked, and how often data is reported.

A meter maintains rules specifying accountable entities (the subject of accounting, such as a user or a host) and how to classify each packet. Using rolling counters (where counts continue to accumulate across reports) allows data loss recovery and provides continuity checks. Flows are marked idle when no packets arrive for a configured inactivity timeout, allowing the meter to reclaim memory.
sections.eli5: A flow is just a group of packets that look similar. The meter counts them. You can choose to make many small flows or a few big ones depending on how much detail you need.

sections.title: Meter Function and Packet Matching
sections.content:
When a packet arrives at a meter, the meter extracts attribute values (source address, destination address, port numbers, etc.) to form a match key. This key is tested against the meter's rule set — a program running in a pattern matching engine — which determines whether the packet should be counted, ignored, or handled specially.

Crucially, the rule set determines a flow key, which identifies the flow the packet belongs to. The meter looks up the flow in its flow table; if the flow is not present it creates a new entry, then increments the appropriate counters (forward or reverse depending on packet direction).

Packets may match in both directions (forward and reverse), which the meter must handle carefully to avoid double-counting. The meter uses a well-defined algorithm: it tries to match in the forward direction, then in reverse, and increments the appropriate counter. This design allows rule sets to specify flows in forward direction only and lets the meter handle bidirectional traffic automatically.
sections.eli5: When a packet arrives, the meter checks its addresses and ports against rules. The rules say which flow it belongs to. The meter then adds it to that flow's count.

sections.title: Data Collection and System Management
sections.content:
Meters store accumulated flow data in a flow table. Periodically, a meter reader collects this data — either by uploading the entire table or by reading individual records via a data transfer protocol. The meter reader may collect from multiple meters, and multiple meter readers may collect from the same meter for redundancy.

A manager configures each meter with flow specifications (which traffic to measure), control parameters (flow table size, inactivity timeout, sampling rate), and current rule set. The manager also controls meter readers, specifying which meters to read from, how often to read, and which attributes to collect. Multiple managers can manage a network's measurement infrastructure.

The architecture is designed for flexibility: meters continue running if a meter reader fails; they accumulate data until the reader restarts. Collections from different meter readers need not be synchronized. The rule set ID is recorded with each flow record so that changes in measurement rules can be tracked and understood in the analysis phase.
sections.eli5: The reader periodically asks the meter for its counts. The manager tells the reader when to collect and tells the meter what to count. They work together to gather the data that analysis applications need.
